question: Which way does time flow in a case-control study?
explanation: You've got this! Case-control studies start with people who already have the condition (the outcome) and look back in time to see what caused it (the exposure). [learn more](GST114_U2_T19#GST114_U2_T19_h1)

question: Why is a case-control study called 'observational' instead of 'experimental'?

options.A: Data is collected exclusively through laboratory microscope observation
options.B: Researchers do not manipulate or assign treatments to participants
options.C: Participants observe their own health outcomes during the trial
options.D: The study takes place only in a controlled hospital ward setting

explanation: Great thinking! In observational studies, we simply watch and record what naturally happens without interfering or giving treatments ourselves. [learn more](GST114_U2_T19#GST114_U2_T19_h1)

question: At the very start of a case-control study, how are participants grouped?

options.A: Based on their socioeconomic status and income level
options.B: Based on whether they have the disease or not
options.C: Based on whether they received a vaccine or not
options.D: Based on their willingness to participate in research

explanation: Spot on! The magic of a case-control study begins by separating people into two groups: those with the disease (cases) and those without it (controls). [learn more](GST114_U2_T19#GST114_U2_T19_h2)

question: A researcher picks participants based on whether they were exposed to a risk factor, then follows them forward. What study is this?
explanation: You're doing great! Starting with exposure and following people forward into the future defines a cohort study, not a case-control study. [learn more](GST114_U2_T19#GST114_U2_T19_h2)

question: What is the golden rule when choosing control subjects for a case-control study?

options.A: They must have a milder form of the disease being studied
options.B: They must be medical professionals working in the same hospital
options.C: They must come from the same source population as the cases
options.D: They must be younger than the patients selected as cases

explanation: Makes total sense, right? For a fair comparison, your controls need to come from the exact same background community as your cases. [learn more](GST114_U2_T19#GST114_U2_T19_h3)

question: Why can using healthy neighbors as controls for hospitalized patients mess up study results?

options.A: They refuse to answer questions regarding past food consumption
options.B: They are guaranteed to develop the disease later in the year
options.C: Their health-seeking behaviors and baseline access to care differ
options.D: They are usually much older than the hospitalized patient group

explanation: You've got this! People who go to the hospital often have different health habits or access to care than healthy people walking around the neighborhood. [learn more](GST114_U2_T19#GST114_U2_T19_h3)

question: What does 'recall bias' mean in a case-control study?

options.A: Researchers forgetting to record the laboratory results of study subjects
options.B: Participants refusing to sign informed consent documentation before the interview
options.C: Sick patients remembering past exposures differently than healthy controls
options.D: Computers deleting electronic hospital records due to sudden power outages

explanation: Think of it this way: when someone gets sick, they naturally search their memory hard for what caused it, which can make them report past habits differently than healthy people. [learn more](GST114_U2_T19#GST114_U2_T19_h4)

question: How do researchers stop 'observer bias' during interviews?

options.A: By changing the diagnostic criteria halfway through the data collection
options.B: By allowing cases to interview themselves using online forms
options.C: By excluding all participants who cannot remember their medical history
options.D: By ensuring interviewers do not know if the participant is a case or control

explanation: Brilliant! Keeping interviewers 'blind' to who is sick and who is healthy stops them from accidentally guiding or probing the sick patients more. [learn more](GST114_U2_T19#GST114_U2_T19_h4)

question: What is the main statistical value calculated in a case-control study?
explanation: Easy and straightforward! Because we already know who is sick, the odds ratio is our go-to mathematical tool for measuring the association. [learn more](GST114_U2_T19#GST114_U2_T19_h5)

question: An odds ratio comes out to 0.35 for a certain diet. What does this tell us?

options.A: The exposure is associated with a lower chance of developing the disease
options.B: The exposure increases the risk of getting sick by thirty-five percent
options.C: There is no statistical connection between the food and the illness
options.D: The study calculation contains a major error and must be repeated

explanation: You're crushing it! An odds ratio well below 1 means the exposure actually protects against the disease—it lowers the odds! [learn more](GST114_U2_T19#GST114_U2_T19_h5)

question: What is a 'confounding variable' in research?

options.A: A software glitch that corrupts the statistical data table
options.B: A laboratory error caused by using expired chemical reagents
options.C: An unmeasured third factor that distorts the true exposure-disease relationship
options.D: A patient who refuses to answer questions during the nurse interview

explanation: Think of a confounder as a sneaky third factor that muddies the waters, making a relationship look stronger or weaker than it really is. [learn more](GST114_U2_T19#GST114_U2_T19_h6)

question: At what point in a study do researchers use 'matching' to control for confounding variables?

options.A: During the final data interpretation phase
options.B: During the laboratory specimen culture phase
options.C: After the research paper has been published

explanation: Spot on! Matching things like age or gender between cases and controls is a smart strategy planned right at the very beginning of the study. [learn more](GST114_U2_T19#GST114_U2_T19_h6)

question: What is a major advantage of running a case-control study?

options.A: It proves absolute cause and effect without error
options.B: It calculates true population disease incidence directly
options.C: It is highly efficient for studying rare diseases
options.D: It eliminates all forms of human recall bias entirely

explanation: You've got this! Instead of following thousands of healthy people for years, we start with people who already have the rare condition, saving time and resources. [learn more](GST114_U2_T19#GST114_U2_T19_h7)

question: Why can it sometimes be tricky to prove which came first (temporality) in a case-control study?

options.A: Control subjects are rarely matched properly to the age profile of cases
options.B: Participants change their answers to match the hypotheses of the nursing researchers
options.C: Data on past exposures is collected retrospectively after the disease has already occurred
options.D: Laboratory tests are unable to detect microorganisms after twenty-four hours

explanation: Makes total sense! Because we look backward after the illness has struck, it can sometimes be tough to prove for sure that the exposure happened before the disease. [learn more](GST114_U2_T19#GST114_U2_T19_h7)

question: During a sudden disease outbreak, why do public health teams quickly use a case-control study?

options.A: To calculate the lifetime medical costs of chronic illness
options.B: To evaluate nursing staff performance on hospital wards
options.C: To test new surgical procedures in a teaching hospital
options.D: To identify the source of infection and halt transmission

explanation: Brilliant! In an outbreak, every minute counts. Case-control studies help us quickly track down the source of infection so we can stop the spread. [learn more](GST114_U2_T19#GST114_U2_T19_h8)

question: If a community has a sudden cholera outbreak, who should investigators interview as controls?

options.A: Healthy individuals born ten years after the outbreak occurred
options.B: Healthy people from the same community who attended the same events
options.C: Patients admitted to a distant hospital for unrelated surgical operations
options.D: Healthcare workers who were on vacation outside the affected region

explanation: You're a natural! Controls must come from the exact same community background and share similar risks to give us a fair, accurate comparison. [learn more](GST114_U2_T19#GST114_U2_T19_h8)
